brittle faulting was induced in a rock sequence that was undergoing predominantly ductile deformation.
brittle faulting was caused by ductile deformation and that this process was responsible for the development of a fault zone.

In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of ductile deformation in controlling the development of brittle faults and the evolution of the structural and metamorphic history of the footwall of an extensional fault in a continental margin.

(1) the development of a model for the formation of brittle faults during extensional denuda- tion, (2) the role of rheological stratigraphy in the development of such faults, and (3) the role of ductile deformation in the formation of brittle fault zones.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ductile deformation of the mylonitic rocks caused the brittle faulting in this area of the Turtleback fault zone.

brittle faulting was directly induced by ductile shear strain, and that this brittle faulting occurred at different times and in different rocks as the result of the variable ductile deformation history of the lower plate.
ductile deformation of the footwall rocks was directly responsible for the brittle faulting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
brittle faulting is a direct consequence of ductile deformation.
the Badwater Turtlebacks are examples of a fault that formed by progressive deformation of an initially ductile rock sequence during a period of extension.
brittle faulting in this area is a result of the rheological stratification and ductile deformation of the lower plate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ductile deformation in the lower plate can induce brittle faulting in overlying rocks that are less ductile.
ductile deformation in a heterogeneous rock sequence can cause brittle faulting in adjacent, weaker rock layers.

the brittle faulting that occurred at the Badwater Turtle back fault was directly related to the ductile deformation of the footwall rocks and was not a response to the development of an underlying brittle detachment fault.
